item.title: Chattogram hosts final of next year’s Women’s U19 T20 World Cup
item.description:
Bangladesh will play the United Arab Emirates in Sylhet on the opening day of the ICC Women’s U19 T20 World Cup, which Bangladesh and Nepal will co-host from January 21 next year.
The International Cricket Council released the full schedule on Wednesday. The final will be played in Chattogram on February 6, and the city will also host both semi-finals on February 4.
Only the semi-finals and the final have reserve days.
The tournament will be played at four venues, two in each country. Sylhet and Chattogram will stage 12 matches each, while Mulpani will host eight and Kirtipur seven. The two Nepal grounds will hold group matches and some Super Six games.
Eight teams will be in action on the opening day, with two matches each in Sylhet and Mulpani. Play will start at 9:30am and 1:30pm local time.
Bangladesh are in Group C with Australia, the UAE and Nigeria, and will play all three group matches in Sylhet. After facing the UAE, they meet Australia on January 23 and Nigeria on January 25.
Two-time champions India are in Group A with Ireland, Nepal and West Indies. Pakistan will take on New Zealand, Samoa and South Africa in Group B, while the USA, Scotland, England and Sri Lanka make up Group D.
The group stage ends on January 26. The top three teams from each group go through to the Super Six, where qualifiers from Groups A and D form one group and those from Groups B and C the other.
Each team plays two Super Six matches, and the top two from each group reach the semi-finals.
India won the inaugural edition in South Africa in 2023, beating England in the final, and kept the title in Malaysia in 2025 with a win over South Africa.
Bangladesh reached the Super Six in both editions but have never played in a semi-final.

item.title: The UN’s latest climate change report is spotlighting the U.S., and not for a good reason
item.description:
Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.

“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.

The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries’ climate fighting plans. He wasn’t part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound.

Shooting far past Paris climate goal

The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection.

Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.

The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”

Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.

“The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn’t part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”

An added tenth of a degree of danger

Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.

“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”

Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.

And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.

“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

item.title: BBC layoffs: More jobs slashed, channels cut as British broadcaster faces ‘immediate cost pressures’
item.description:
Media companies continue to struggle as consumers pivot away from traditional forms of content. 

The latest example comes from the BBC, which has announced it will cut over 100 jobs. The U.K.-based broadcaster is attempting to save £500 million ($670 million) over the next two years. 

BBC is primarily funded by a licensing fee, a £180 annual payment that provides viewers with all TV channels, streaming services, and more. It’s designed to keep the BBC “free of advertisements and independent of shareholder and political interest” in the U.K. 

However, the number of TV licenses sold has shrunk in recent years. 

“We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world,” BBC director-general Matt Brittin said in a statement. “We all know that means tough choices.” 

Channels and archive radio network cut

In pursuit of this mission, the BBC will also stop broadcasting BBC Scotland and BBC Three, a channel geared toward younger audiences, come spring. It’s further cutting archive radio network Radio 4 Extra, with its content available on the BBC Sounds app. 

“Axing these TV channels and Radio 4 Extra may make business sense in a world where audiences are increasingly finding their BBC content on-demand, but I understand it saves less than 10 million pounds a year, a tiny fraction of what’s needed,” BBC News culture and media editor Katie Razzall said in a broadcast. “So far, the BBC has announced 200 million pounds in savings; it needs to find another 300 million pounds more.” 

The BBC plans to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs over the next couple years. It already slashed 550 positions in June. 

“There is a bigger fight going on here,” Razzall elaborated in an article. “The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future—and how it will be paid for. It won’t harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient.” 

Rachel Jupp, director of BBC News, will be announcing more savings plans in early 2027. 

Reached for comment, a BBC spokesperson referred Fast Company to its press release about the latest cuts.

BBC Three commissioned popular shows such as Fleabag, Killing Eve, and Normal People. Despite cutting its broadcast, the BBC Three team is receiving more money for commissions targeting audiences aged 16 to 34. 

BBC Scotland and BBC Three will be available on BBC iPlayer, the company’s online streamer, along with other platforms such as YouTube. BBC Scotland’s programs will also air on BBC One or BBC Two in the country, but the channel’s nightly News at Seven will stop running. According to the BBC, 12% of Scots watched BBC Scotland last year.

item.title: Netflix’s stock just collapsed to a 2-year low: Is the streaming giant’s ad business in trouble?
item.description:
Shares in Netflix Inc. (Nasdaq: NFLX) have fallen to a more than a two-year low after the streaming giant posted its Q3 2026 results yesterday.

Despite hitting Wall Street’s projected revenue target of nearly $12.9 billion for the quarter, an update on the company’s increasingly critical ad business dampened investor optimism, sinking the stock with it. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

Yesterday, Netflix announced its results for its third quarter of fiscal 2026. Unfortunately for the company, those results—and Netflix’s guidance—were somewhat of a mixed bag.

There was good news: Revenue for the quarter totaled $12.87 billion, representing 11.8% year-over-year growth.

The company’s diluted earnings per share also reached 87 cents. As noted by CNBC, this means Netflix hit the revenue target investors were expecting and exceeded EPS expectations by five cents per share.

However, there was also plenty of news that gave investors pause—and that has caused the stock to drop significantly in premarket trading today.

What did Netflix project?

For the fourth quarter, Netflix said it expects revenue to grow by about 11.5% to $13.44 billion. Double-digit growth is nothing to sneeze at, but unfortunately for Netflix, that revenue forecast comes in under the $13.51 billion that Wall Street was expecting, notes TipRanks. 

When it comes to its full fiscal 2026 guidance, Netflix says it now expects revenue of $51.1 billion. As with its Q4 forecast, that is a double-digit increase (about 13% year over year), but it is also on the lower end of the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range Netflix previously forecast for fiscal 2026.

But perhaps what spooked investors most of all was the updated guidance for Netflix’s ad business. The company said it now expects full-year 2026 ad revenue to be around $2.7 billion. That’s $300 million, or 10% less, than the $3 billion in ad revenue Netflix had previously forecast.

What’s weighing on Netflix’s ad business?

As most Netflix subscribers will have noticed, the company has been raising prices on its ad-free subscriptions for years. But Netflix isn’t stupid. It knows that price rises mean consumers’ pocketbooks will be hit harder.

However, Netflix also believes that by jacking up ad-free subscription costs, it will cause many cost-conscious consumers not to cancel their subscriptions, but instead to opt for lower-cost, ad-supported tiers.

While these lower-priced subscriptions mean Netflix will extract less up-front revenue from subscribers, over the long run, Netflix should make more money from each subscriber by serving them ads.

Netflix isn’t alone in this. Nearly every major streaming service has introduced ad-supported tiers in recent years in hopes of transitioning more users to them in order to boost their bottom lines.

In the industry, ad-supported subscriptions are seen as a way for streamers to boost revenue. Investors, too, have put significant hopes for revenue growth into ad-supported tiers.

That’s why investors were so disheartened to hear Netflix announce that its total full-year 2026 ad revenue is expected to come in 10% lower than previously forecast. 

As for one of the primary causes of the ad forecast reduction, Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said it was due to a slower launch of some ad products than originally expected.

“[S]pecifically in this case, we’ve seen some delays in the rollout and partner integrations for some of those new ads products,” Peters said on the company’s financial call, according to a PitchBook transcript. “So getting to the integration model that we want sometimes takes a bit more work with our partners, but we strongly believe that a modest short-term hit for a better long-term strategic position is a good ultimate tradeoff.”

Peters added that the slower rollout shouldn’t impact long-term gains, but investors tend to think in quarters, not the long term. And the lower ad forecast helped drive Netflix stock lower as well.

How have NFLX shares reacted?

As of the time of this writing, NFLX shares are down more than 6.4% to $64.23 in premarket trading. That’s after the company’s shares closed down 1.66% yesterday to $68.69.

Netflix’s current premarket price of around $64 per share is an ignominious milestone for the company. Its share price has not been that low since August 2024—more than two years ago. 

Even before today’s 6.4% drop, Netflix’s stock price was trading down more than 26% for the year.

Over the past year, the stock’s price has declined a staggering 44.5% as of yesterday’s close, according to data from Yahoo Finance.

Where the stock goes next is anyone’s guess, but investors will clearly be keeping an eye on the company’s ad efforts in the quarters ahead—efforts Peters seems to have faith in.

“[U]ltimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that’s a big mechanism of growth for us,” he told analysts on yesterday’s call. “So we are very focused on getting those out to them as quickly as we possibly can.”

Correction: Netflix’s previous 2026 guidance was in the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range, not $15.0 to $15.4 billion range as an earlier version of this article stated.

item.title: Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030?
item.description:
Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030? Expert comment thilton.drupal 22 October 2026

Egyptian president’s surprise announcement comes amid deep economic difficulties and includes a plan for a military-approved succession.

Egypt’s President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi has declared he will step down at the end of his third term in 2030. Speaking during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation on 17 October, he also outlined a military-centric succession process to select the next president and senior officials beyond 2030. 

The statement surprised many observers, and perhaps even state officials. If Sisi follows through on his pledge and leaves peacefully, he’d be the first Egyptian president to leave office without dying, being imprisoned or facing a popular uprising. 

The unprecedented decision will have significant implications for Egypt’s political landscape, the balance of power within the regime and the military’s influence over politics and governance.

Why is Sisi leaving?

Sisi became president in 2014, after the overthrow of Mohamed Morsi’s short-lived Muslim Brotherhood government. He is currently serving his third term, after winning elections seen as predetermined in 2018 and 2023. A constitutional referendum in 2019, also seen as predetermined, increased the president’s term from four to six years, extending Sisi’s current term to 2030.

Sisi, who is 71, did not give an exact reason for why he would step down in his speech at the military academy. He said that there would be no further amendments to Egypt’s constitution to prolong his rule and declared it ‘a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed,’ suggesting a transition of power is inevitable.  

Economic troubles

Two factors likely lie behind this surprise decision. 

First, the debt-financed economic model pursued under Sisi is unsustainable. This system has sustained military dominance and stalled urgent economic reform. The government’s vast borrowing to fund mega projects has created a structural economic crisis. 

In this year’s budget, debt servicing accounts for 63.9 per cent of planned expenditure, a significant increase from 43 per cent in 2014. Interest payments alone, as a share of GDP, exceed the combined allocations for education, healthcare, wages and subsidies combined. Egypt’s external debt rose from $46.1 billion in 2014 (16.4 per cent of GDP) to $164.8 billion (38.9 per cent of GDP) by the end of Q1 2026. 

The Egyptian pound exchange rate has plummeted from 7.14 per dollar in mid-2014 to about 53.8 per dollar in October 2026. Urban inflation has risen from 8.3 per cent in May 2014 to 13.9 per cent in September 2026 and is expected to rise further. 

This increased pressure on ordinary Egyptians has made the last decade one of plummeting living standards. Official data shows the national poverty rate has reached 35.7 per cent in 2023.

Public anger over rising living costs, combined with structural imbalances and rising debt, have made Sisi’s economic policies untenable – even among his allies.

The long-lasting economic crisis is an existential threat to the regime’s stability. Sisi himself may have calculated that Egypt urgently needs a new social contract to avoid economic-driven social unrest that could push him out or plunge the country into perpetual chaos. 

He will likely want to avoid the fate of President Hosni Mubarak, who was forced to leave office amid the January 25 Revolution in 2011. It is also likely that there will be an arrangement to protect Sisi and his family members from potential future prosecutions as a condition of him stepping down. 

Protecting the state 

The second factor relates to Sisi’s vision for his presidency and the state. This is fundamentally shaped by the 2011 uprising, which he has described as ‘the death certificate of the Egyptian state.’ 

Since he was sworn in in 2014, Sisi has repeatedly warned that another popular uprising would threaten the state’s existence. He has portrayed national prosperity as depending on excluding from Egypt’s politics what he frequently calls ‘ahl elshar’ (people of evil), often understood as referring to Islamists. He has also warned of threats to ‘national memory’ on social media. 

Sisi has portrayed it as his – and the military’s – national duty to spare Egypt the chaos engulfing other Arab Spring countries by removing the Muslim Brotherhood from power amid a popular uprising. He has indicated that he considers it his duty to reshape Egypt’s politics to guarantee long-term stability as he sees it.   

In his speech at the military academy, Sisi revealed that he had insisted on incorporating Article 200 into the 2019 constitutional amendments. This article effectively designates the military as the guardian of Egypt’s national, secular identity and the regime. 

Given this, Sisi may therefore feel that departing in 2030 is in line with his aims. The military-trained officials he has designated as his successors would serve as the practical implementers of this vision.

Military-shaped succession

Alongside his plans to step down, Sisi also announced that the armed forces will fund a 30-month military academy course to train potential future leaders. Egyptians will then be able to ‘elect and choose’ from among the graduates.

The course will train select candidates, who must have a PhD and be 40-50 years old, for positions including minister, member of parliament, governor, and potentially even president. Those who have served in government for at least six years will be exempted. 

Sisi’s choice of the military academy is not surprising, since it has long been tasked with promoting a military-centric nationalism and overseeing appointments and promotions in state institutions. This has sometimes sparked resistance, for example from judges in January. 

In effect, the system will replace the electoral process with competence criteria, narrowing the pool of trusted candidates and excluding anyone who is ‘tendentious, a traitor, or a criminal’ from becoming president. 

Future implications

Although this process finally paves the way for civilians to become president, the military will likely retain decisive influence over leadership selection and the state’s strategic direction. The military’s constitutional mandate means its commanders’ views and preferences would continue to shape key state decisions.

Related work

Should Egypt join the Mecca Pact?

In this setup, Sisi will likely retain entrenched loyalties and broader political influence. The changes could establish an informal military guardianship model that sits above the president and government beyond 2030. This might resemble Turkey in the 1990s.

The new government training system might also invite challenges. It seems designed to side-line dissidents, the Muslim Brotherhood and rival generals. But by effectively excluding individuals without a postgraduate degree or those who fail to secure academy approval, it might be deemed unconstitutional and face legal challenges. It could also spark fierce competition among key security branches.

Will Sisi reconsider?

Sisi’s decision to step down might face resistance from key institutions and influential figures in his patronage system, who may try to convince him to reconsider to protect their interests. 

These attempts may intensify if Egypt’s military becomes involved in escalating regional conflicts. Sisi recently sought authorization from parliament to deploy troops to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. 

If living conditions worsen and social unrest breaks out, Sisi may conclude that staying in power best guarantees stability for Egypt. 

Potential for civilian rule?

Despite its risks, Sisi’s decision may facilitate a transition towards a less authoritarian government in the long term. It took Egyptians 15 years after the 2011 uprising to hear an Egyptian president pledge an ordinary, peaceful transition of power. 

By declaring he will step down, Sisi could end up kickstarting a tradition in which no single ruler stays in power until death. Civilians might finally be seen as capable rulers. 

This will not happen overnight, of course. It would depend on Sisi keeping his word and social stability holding until 2030. But if this is the case, the military guardianship Sisi is establishing may, in the long term, be seen as a transitional period toward a more stable, more open and freer society.

item.title: Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine?
item.description:
Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine? Expert comment jon.wallace 22 October 2026

Not immediately. But a Democratic victory could set the terms for a new approach by the next president.

Whatever the results, November’s midterm elections will not immediately transform US policy toward Israel and Palestine. In any outcome, the separation of powers means that President Donald Trump will still control American foreign policy. Even a Democrat-controlled Congress could not compel his administration to pursue a fundamentally different approach. 

But the midterms may accelerate a transformation that is already underway in the Democratic Party and among the US electorate, where the political centre of gravity on Israel and Palestine is shifting rapidly. 

If Democrats win a majority in either or both houses, they will gain new congressional tools to act on Israel–Palestine issues. Most importantly, the legislation they put forward would establish the policy baseline from which a future Democratic administration would govern.

The shift

Among dozens of others, Democrats like Abdul El-Sayed, running for the US Senate in Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres, running in the general against another Democrat in California, have drawn considerable attention for their criticism of Israeli government actions – and US support for them. The race in Michigan, which could be decisive for Democratic hopes to retake the senate, looks tight.

But even if progressive candidates don’t do as well as expected in these elections, a shift is underway. Developments in Washington over just the past month illustrate how much has already changed.

On 29 September, 46 of 47 Senate Democrats voted for a resolution led by Senators Chris Van Hollen, Tim Kaine and Bernie Sanders. This would ‘require the Department of State to provide information and assessments related to investigations of the killing of United States citizens by violent Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces in the West Bank’. The resolution did not pass the Republican majority. But the vote was remarkable for its unanimity. Such Democratic unity on a resolution critical of Israel would have been almost unimaginable only a few years ago.

The vote follows a distinct trajectory in Democratic politics. When Senator Bernie Sanders forced the Senate to vote on blocking weapon sales to Israel in November 2024, only 18 Democrat senators supported him. This April, 40 of 47 Senate Democrats voted against a sale of bulldozers to Israel. And 36 opposed the sale of 1,000-pound bombs. Now, with the September resolution, virtually the entire Senate Democratic caucus has voted to demand accountability from Israel.

Become a corporate member

Give your organization access to trusted geopolitical analysis, policy insight and expert networks to help leaders anticipate risk, navigate uncertainty and make informed decisions.

Then came the House of Representatives. On 1 October, Rep. Joaquin Castro and other members introduced the Stop the Settlements Act. This builds on the Biden administration’s 2024 sanctions on violent Israeli extremists in the West Bank, which saw a major power set up a process to sanction those undermining peace and threatening violence in the West Bank. 

It also builds on the subsequent 2026 sanctions by European countries and Canada against products originating in Israeli settlements. The Act would impose sanctions on individuals and entities responsible for building or expanding Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank or Gaza and prohibit settlement goods from entering the US market. 

These developments point toward an emerging Democratic Party position: one that more actively defends the rights of the Palestinian people and is more willing to seek to compel Israel and the White House to move in that direction. Notably, Barack Obama’s planned 24 October event with El-Sayed on the campaign trail shows a greater willingness by the party’s elite to accommodate criticism of Israeli policies.

That shift matters. Israel and Palestine remain secondary issues for most US voters, compared to the economy, healthcare, education and other domestic concerns. But firm convictions on Israel–Palestine have become important attributes for some candidates in Democratic party politics. And the midterms will, in some ways, be a referendum on how criticism of Israeli policies affects voter intentions – with candidates like El-Sayed calling Israeli actions in Gaza a genocide, a claim the Netanyahu government strenuously denies. 

But one thing looks certain: US views on the Israeli government have become less favourable across age groups and political parties. Even among American Jews, 61 per cent believe Israel is guilty of war crimes and 39 per cent call it genocide, according to a 2025 Washington Post poll. The tide may already have decisively shifted, regardless of whether or not candidates like El-Sayed win their races. 

A Democratic Congress

Democratic takeover of the House and the Senate would make the shift more consequential immediately. Much of Congress’s influence over foreign policy occurs not through dramatic floor votes, but through the accumulation of hearings, letters, reporting requirements, funding restrictions and private pressure on administrations. 

Democratic-controlled committees could hold hearings on settlement expansion in the West Bank and settler violence, scrutinize US arms sales to Israel, demand administration briefings, investigate the treatment of American citizens, mark-up legislation and use appropriations and oversight to press the executive branch. 

House and Senate Democrats should begin laying the groundwork to create an affirmative American Palestine policy. That is, a policy not only defined by a move to restrict Israeli settlement-building and the sale of weapons to Israel, but one that advocates for Palestinian self-determination and an architecture for advancing it. 

Over the decades, Congress has constructed a dense web of laws that restrict American relations with the PLO and the Palestinian Authority. A Democratic Congress could therefore begin to map those restrictions and decide how to address them. Which can be addressed administratively? Which need Congressional amendment or repeal? What policy changes will the US seek from the Palestinian leadership? 

This will not be straightforward: Democrats are still debating these policies, and unanimity will not always be possible: there remains a diversity of views and priorities within the party. 

Congress also needs far greater exposure to Palestinian political, economic and civil-society leaders. While many US politicians routinely engage with every dimension of Israeli politics, few have sustained relationships with Palestinians who can explain Palestinian institutions, aspirations and internal debates.

Two time horizons

Were candidates like El-Sayed to lose their races, and were midterms results to be disappointing for the Democrats, it is possible that some in the party might hesitate about the trajectory on Israel and Palestine policy.

But, assuming Democrats gain control of Congress, they could use 2027 and 2028 to constrain, oversee and prepare. A Democratic Congress could press Israel for accountability for violence against Palestinians and Americans, challenge settlement expansion, scrutinize US military assistance, support viable elements of Gaza reconstruction, strengthen Palestinian institutions and begin removing legal obstacles to normal US-Palestinian relations.

These preparations will be significant if a Democrat returns to the White House in 2029. A new administration will be best able to move forward a markedly different policy if significant progress is made in the previous two years.

In this respect, though the midterms will not be the moment US policy toward Israel and Palestine changes, they can set the context for any Democrat running in the presidential primaries – which essentially begin as soon as the new Congress is seated. 

Those who have been advocating for Palestinian rights for decades now see that not only their elected representatives, but the next US president may align with them as well. 

That will not fix anything today for the relatives of the more than 70,000 Palestinians killed in Gaza, the millions that continue to suffer in the occupied territories, or Israelis dealing with the aftermath of the Hamas cross-border attacks of 7 October 2023. But it does provide a modicum of hope that there is a pathway to freedom and liberty for all. What we’ll learn from the US midterms is how quickly that change is likely to come.

Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump

Historical comparisons are always inexact. No one conflict precisely mirrors another. Yet Donald Trump’s shameless appeasement of Vladimir Putin carries more than a noxious whiff of Neville Chamberlain’s failed attempt in Munich in 1938 to head off war with Nazi Germany. To be fair to the former UK prime minister – and history largely hasn’t been – his peacemaking efforts had the enthusiastic backing of most people in Britain and France who, like him, were desperate to avoid a repeat of the horrors of the first world war. Trump enjoys no equivalent public support for his treachery. Nor does he face the prospect of a US war with Russia. His betrayal of Ukraine is cynically self-interested, globally dangerous and utterly contemptible.

US-Russian talks on agreeing the shoddy terms of a precedent-setting American sell-out of Ukraine are at an advanced stage, after meetings in St Petersburg this week. Trump has zigzagged over the war ever since returning to office. Now, panicked by record-low poll ratings, he seems determined to scapegoat Ukraine and force its de facto capitulation. Recent steps – his shocking decision to fund Putin’s war machine by buying Russian diesel, his waiving of tougher sanctions, his mysterious, lethal interruptions in US satellite and intelligence sharing with Kyiv, and his renewed attempt to oust Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – mark Trump out as the skulking Judas, the craven Brutus of the modern age. Hybrid Threats: Why Awareness Must Transcend Individual Cyberattacks
item.description:
Every October, Cybersecurity Awareness Month puts practical security measures in the spotlight. Can an employee recognize a phishing email? Will someone pause before clicking a suspicious link? Are passwords and access credentials being protected? These are important questions; individual behaviors are crucial to maintaining cybersecurity.

But awareness is so laser focused on preventing and mitigating the malicious cyberattack, it’s easy to lose sight of the bigger picture: the cyberattack in front of you may be only one piece of the threat.

In the era of hybrid threats, a cyberattack could be part of a broader campaign in which digital activity intersects with cognitive warfare, sabotage, unusual drone activity, disruptions to communications and navigation systems, and much more. State and state-linked networks might use online fraud or scams to generate revenue for operations, launder funds and undermine confidence in financial and/or government institutions.

The challenge for security and law enforcement agencies transcends detecting and responding to one cyber incident at a time. They must also determine whether events that appear separate may be connected.

That distinction changes what it means to be aware, and the urgency is intensifying. Recent research and reporting shows Russian cyber activity directed at European targets is likely intended to enable intelligence collection, operational reach and long-term access rather than immediate disruption. In parallel, the Iranian government is believed to be relying on a longstanding hybrid warfare model combining cyber operations, asymmetric military operations, information warfare, proxy attacks and coercive state activity, with AI increasingly acting as a force multiplier.

Expect to see more of this going forward, not less.

CONNECTING THE DOTS

Consider the signals individually: a government agency experiences a cyberattack. Unusual drone activity is reported over critical infrastructure. GPS service is disrupted. False or misleading information is deliberately spread. Viewed on their own, these events may have different causes, and each can appear to be a separate incident.

Yet hybrid campaigns often depend on individual activities initially looking ambiguous or unrelated. If each signal is treated only as a self-contained incident, relevant connections may be missed – and when the connections are missed, so is the broader pattern they could form.

This does not make traditional cybersecurity awareness less important. It makes awareness more demanding. The familiar focus on individual judgment must be matched by institutional awareness: the ability of government agencies, armed forces, critical infrastructure operators, and other relevant organizations to recognize which signals may matter beyond the immediate event.

That begins before advanced analysis enters the picture. An organization cannot share information it did not capture, and it cannot capture information it did not recognize as potentially relevant. The first requirement is therefore a common understanding of what may be security-relevant and what information is needed to contribute to a broader situational picture.

This shift is central to the awareness challenge. A suspicious link has a clear place in the traditional conversation. A weak signal in a hybrid environment may not have the same clarity. Its significance may emerge only when it is considered alongside other information. Awareness, in this context, means looking beyond the apparent boundaries of a single incident without assuming that any one event tells the entire story.

The sequence matters: recognize, capture, share, assess. If a potentially relevant signal drops out at any stage, it cannot inform the larger picture. If it moves through that sequence, it becomes one piece of information that can be examined in relation to others.

The next task is to bring those fragmented pieces together. Threat intelligence, decision intelligence and artificial intelligence can help teams work across large volumes of data, correlate information, reveal connections, and alert analysts to anomalies. Their value is especially clear when no single signal is decisive. Several weak and seemingly unrelated signals may form a pattern that supports a more informed assessment of the security situation.

The point is not simply to accumulate more data. It is to make relevant information usable as part of a coherent view. A list of isolated incidents still leaves decision-makers looking at fragments. A situational picture asks a different set of questions: What may connect these events? What does the combined pattern suggest? Which developments deserve closer attention? And what might happen next?

That last question is essential. The goal is not limited to identifying a cyberattack or another security-relevant event after it occurs. It is to understand the relationships among relevant signals well enough to identify potential future developments at an early stage. Detection remains necessary, but detection without connection can leave the larger threat out of view.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, this broader perspective offers a useful way to expand the conversation. At the individual level, awareness still means recognizing the suspicious email, protecting credentials, avoiding scams and frauds and thinking before clicking. At the national level, it also means making sure the right organizations know what to notice, what to record, what to share, and how to place that information in context.

The difference is one of scale. An individual may be watching for a malicious link. Government agencies, armed forces, critical infrastructure operators, and other relevant organizations must also be watching for relationships among cyber activity, disinformation, sabotage, drone activity and communications interference.

That is the blind spot Cybersecurity Awareness Month should help bring into focus. There’s more to awareness than paying attention before clicking a link. Awareness means we know which signals deserve attention, whether we can bring them together, and whether we can see the threat they may form before the pattern becomes unmistakable.

item.title: Millions removed from India's draft voter rolls viewed as targeting of Muslims
item.description:
Millions removed from India's draft voter rolls viewed as targeting of Muslims

Submitted by Muheet Ul Islam on Fri, 10/23/2026 - 15:54
Over 100 million people have been removed from the voter list, and many are questioning why specific communities are overrepresented
A student activist holds a poster while on a bus after getting detained during a protest demanding the resignation of the nation's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities linked to the 'special intensive revision', in New Delhi on 13 October 2026 (Arun Sankar/AFP)
Off

Sameen Ud Din has lived at the same address in Old Delhi for years. He voted in the 2025 Delhi elections. But when the draft voter list for the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, was published this time around, his name was missing.

“It is an irony not to find my name in the SIR list. I did not receive any notice from the Election Commission of India [ECI] when my name was deleted,” Din, a 44-year-old businessman from the Nizam Ud Din area of Old Delhi, told Middle East Eye.

“I am now being asked to fill out Form 6, an application to register as a new voter, which is clearly a false declaration and carries penal consequences,” he added.

Din said he did not know what would happen next and felt pressured to submit the form. India's next general election is in 2029.

But Din is not alone. Muslims in different parts of India have reported similar problems, with countless people finding their names missing from the draft voter lists.

Approximately 133 million names had been flagged for removal from the voter list.

Critics say many eligible voters have been removed, with Muslims and Dalits – Dalits occupy the lowest rung in Hinduism’s caste system – among those mostly affected. 

An investigation from The Wire shows that in West Bengal, out of 2.75 million on the published list of removals, approximately 1.8 million were Muslims - or around 70 percent of the total published "ineligible to vote" list. Muslims make up just 25 percent of that state's electorate.

In some districts, according to The Wire, removals of Muslims made up over 90 percent of the total published removals.

This disparity has also brought protesters onto the streets of New Delhi. At one mid-October protest, India's Congress Party estimated that 250,000 people were present, while tens of thousands have been protesting across the country.

Protests suppressed

The Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, called for demonstrations against the SIR under the slogan “Lehra Do Tiranga” or “Wave the Tricolour”. Protesters carrying national flags gathered at Connaught Place before moving towards Dilli Haat and other parts of central Delhi.

“Gyanesh Kumar, resign”, “Down with Delhi Police”, and “Whenever Modi is scared, he sends the police to the front” were among the other slogans protesters shouted.

'Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics'

- Vishnu, protester

The CJP began in May 2026 as a satirical online movement founded by digital strategist Abhijeet Dipke.

At the time, the movement was demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party or BJP, and the education minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet. The protest came after the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance exams, was leaked; it determines admissions into five-year undergraduate medical courses in India.

It has since developed into a street protest movement.

Today protesters now want the government to stop the SIR and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Figures cited by the ruling BJP show that about 130 million names were dropped from draft voter lists during the revision of the list. The ECI says the deletions are meant to clean up the rolls by removing the names of dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

The protests against these actions took place despite a ban imposed by the BJP-led Delhi government on gatherings of four or more people in some areas. 

The restrictions came after Delhi Police removed Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century observatory and a long-time protest site, from its list of approved protest locations on 12 October. Police named Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as alternative locations.

“We are out to protest to protect democracy. There is no violence going on, but the police are still detaining people. It is illegal. These detentions are a symbol of a fascist state, and this has been happening in India for a long time,” a protester who gave only his first name, Vishnu, told MEE.

He was speaking from a private vehicle hired by Delhi Police to transport detained protesters.

“Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics. They have done it successfully in many places, and we want people to join us and fight this fascist government with us,” he added.

Police detained several CJP leaders and protesters during the demonstrations, including Dipke and All India Students Association president, Neha Bora.

Bora was released on Saturday morning. Dipke appeared before a Special Executive Magistrate court and was released after signing a bond, according to reports. Delhi Police registered at least two cases over the march for violating prohibitory orders.

‘Deleted votes are those of Muslims’ 

On 23 September, The Indian Express published an investigation into alleged irregularities at the Election Commission. The report said the ECI had bypassed legal requirements, raised concerns over the SIR and centralised the voter database.

It also reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders issued without their knowledge, approval or consultation. Their concerns included the addition and deletion of voters, changes to Form 6, access to the electoral database, and the commission’s technology systems.

The ECI rejected claims of an internal rift. It said the notes were suggestions and that every decision taken in the past year, including those related to the SIR, was unanimous. 

Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?
Read More »

For SIR critics, however, the concern goes beyond the Election Commission's functioning. They say the revisions could determine who can vote and, in turn, affect India’s political landscape. 

Ajay Gudavarthy, an associate professor at the Centre for Political Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, said available data on voter deletions suggested that Muslims made up a large share of those removed from the rolls. 

He said he believed the deletions were part of a wider political strategy targeting Muslims and Dalits while building support among Other Backward Class, or OBCs, and upper castes. OBC is an official term employed by the government of India and is an umbrella classification for communities that are deprived or disadvantaged, whether economically, socially or in terms of education. 

“An overwhelming majority of the deleted votes are those of Muslims. This is one reason there is no mass outrage against the SIR. The BJP’s larger design is not only to delete Muslim votes but also to socially polarise people on the basis of these deletions,” Gudavarthy told MEE.

“Alongside Muslims, Dalit votes are also being deleted in order to achieve a reverse consolidation of OBCs and the upper castes,” he added.

The experience of Sayed Rashad Ikmal’s family in Odisha shows how the deletion of names can affect voters at the local level.

Ikmal, a resident of Sungra village in Cuttack district, said the names of his aunt and her husband were missing from the draft SIR voter list, even though his uncle had worked in the finance department of Indian Railways.

“The omission came as a shock to the family, which, like several others in the village, worried about being left off the voter rolls,” Ikmal told MEE.

The family approached the booth-level officer and found that a Form 7 application had been filed with the ECI seeking the deletion of their names. Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name or request the removal of an existing name from the voter roll.

The family later approached the Block Development Officer [BDO], who cancelled the request and restored both names to the SIR list, Ikmal told MEE.

He said the BDO's role was important because local officials could prevent people from being wrongly removed from voter lists. 

India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle
Read More »

“If the BDO does his job honestly, wrongful additions to or deletions from the voter rolls can be stopped, whatever happens at the higher level,” he said.

The residents of Sungra and nearby villages, Ikmal said, had begun to feel that Muslims were being targeted in Odisha. He said these concerns had grown alongside the spread of the “Go to Bangladesh” narrative among people linked to Hindu right-wing groups.

“I describe the threat of being sent to Bangladesh as one of the most intimidating narratives directed at Muslims,” Ikmal said, referring to political claims about Bangladeshi infiltration into Assam and West Bengal.

“The narrative had been used to divide voters ahead of state elections in both states and to build support for the BJP,” he added.

For Gudavarthy, the issue points to a larger question about the strength of India’s democratic institutions.

“The system needs to be made accountable only through mass protests and institutional decentralisation,” he said. “It is a lesson for Indian democracy that institutions can be so easily subverted when there is executive overreach,” he added.

item.title: 'Generational rage': Young Europeans fight to be heard
item.description:
From blockaded schools in Rome to tent camps in Madrid and street protests in France, young people across Europe are turning their anger on a political class they say is not listening.

Their demands vary, but they are united in wanting to make their often marginalised voices heard, sometimes even with radical methods in the face of heavy-handed policing.

“We are fighting and taking our future in our hands,” said Damiano Fusa, 18, a student at Rome’s Cavour high school, the first to be occupied in a wave of student takeovers that has spread across the Italian capital.

“We’re not represented by anyone,” Fusa told AFP, criticising both Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s hard-right coalition and previous centre-left governments for cutting education funding and ignoring young people’s needs.

Hundreds of thousands of high school and university students have rallied in France, Italy, Spain and other European countries in recent weeks, with some protests descending into violence.

Governments have largely focused on restoring order, with France imposing partial curfews and Italy deploying soldiers, responses protesters say obscure their demands and could make things even worse.

“Politicians are responding in ways that are completely disconnected from reality, completely absurd,” said Luis Marques, a 19-year-old psychology student in Lisbon.

Students are demanding action on soaring rents, more spending on education instead of defence and more job opportunities for young people.

But experts say the unrest reflects a broader sense among many young Europeans that they have been shut out of politics and sidelined.

“These young people do not just feel like they do not have a place in politics, they feel they are not being heard at all,” said Geoffrey Pleyers, president of the International Sociological Association.

Rosario Forlenza, a professor at Rome’s Luiss University, called it a “European generational revolt” rooted in a social and economic crisis “to which politicians cannot give a substantive response”.

“Young people are a minority of the population that is shrinking and so their social, economic, cultural, political and electoral weight is becoming ever more irrelevant,” he said.

‘Inspiring other people’

The anger has been particularly palpable in France and Italy, where fresh demonstrations are planned for Saturday.

“People are very angry, they’ve had enough. Working hard all day and still not being able to fill up their shopping cart,” a 20-year-old student who gave his name as Eddy told AFP at a protest in Bordeaux last weekend.

“Will smashing everything change anything? I think it can be a jolt to wake up the politicians. We don’t know what else to do to make ourselves heard. The ballot box? We don’t believe in it anymore,” he said.

Protest movements across Europe are increasingly drawing inspiration from one another, and even looking to youth-led movements further afield in places like Bangladesh, India and Nepal.

In Italy, one student slogan last week urged protesters to “do as in France”, while shared symbols, including the Jolly Roger pirate flag, have become common across youth rallies.

Marcos Navarro, 22, a laboratory quality-control technician from Madrid, said protesters across Europe were meeting to share tactics.

“They’ve come to ask us: ‘How did you do it? How do you organise yourselves?’ We’ve already exchanged ideas,” said Navarro, who has been camping with hundreds of others in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September to protest housing costs and evictions.

Ayla Herrero, a 26-year-old anthropologist helping at the camp’s infirmary, said it was “inspiring for us to know that we’re inspiring other people, that it doesn’t just stay here”.

‘Not acceptable’

Concern about the rise in military spending in Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine has also been a rallying point.

Nikos Mavroudis, a 17-year-old high school student in Athens’ Exarchia neighbourhood, said the money could be better spent on his school, where chunks of plaster are falling.

“It’s not acceptable for classrooms to be dangerous,” said Mavroudis, who hopes to become a cook and plans to move elsewhere in Europe to “countries where things are better”.

At Rome’s occupied Morgagni high school, where students have barricaded entrances with desks, protesters pointed to the crumbling infrastructure as evidence of neglect.

An 18-year-old, who did not want to be named, said the media and politicians in Italy were focusing too heavily on looting and vandalism by some protesters.

“It turns hatred against the students who are victims of this system,” he said.

Asked about the violence, Sabrina Brizzola, 24, coordinator of the Italian University Students’ Union, said organisations like hers should “organise and channel this generational rage”.

“We have shared concerns, even if our ways of protesting differ,” she said.

item.title: UPDF opens fire on tourists, law enforcement personnel in Rangamati's Sajek: ISPR
item.description:
Armed members of the United People's Democratic Front (UPDF) opened fire on tourists and law enforcement in the Gangaram Bazaar area of Sajek, Rangamati district, according to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

The ISPR stated in a press release that the UPDF forcibly used local residents as human shields to block roads.

As a result of the blockage on the Sajek-Baghaihat road, about three thousand tourists visiting Sajek were stranded.

The ISPR press release mentioned that while ensuring the safe passage of tourists, the blockaders created obstacles. In this situation, the Bangladesh Army and police jointly took necessary security measures to ensure the tourists' safe transport to Khagrachari.

While removing the stranded tourists, around 10 AM on Thursday, the blockaders erected barriers in the Gangaram Bazaar area, halting the movement of tourist vehicles. At that time, the army and police patrol team initiated discussions with the blockaders to ensure the safe passage of tourists.

However, during the discussions and around 10: 45 AM, the blockaders, incited by the UPDF, suddenly started throwing stones at law enforcement and targeting tourists, as noted in the statement. To bring the situation under control, the law enforcement used baton charges to disperse the blockaders and resumed the movement of tourist vehicles.

According to the ISPR statement, at approximately 11 AM, it was initially learned that armed UPDF members fired about 30-40 rounds at law enforcement and tourists. During this time, the army patrol team, in self-defense and to ensure the safety of tourists, returned fire, causing the armed individuals to flee the scene. Subsequently, with coordinated efforts by the Bangladesh Army and police, the trapped tourists were evacuated safely, and no casualties were reported.

Preliminary information suggests that the blockade and violence instigated by the UPDF were premeditated. The allegations that locals were coerced into participating in the blockade and being used as human shields are extremely concerning, as mentioned in the statement. It was stated that, due to ongoing security operations in various parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, a faction of UPDF's armed members has taken position in the tourist area.

The statement noted that such violent activities disrupt peace, stability, and public safety in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, and adversely affect the tourism industry and the livelihoods of local people. Especially alarming are incidents endangering the safety of innocent tourists and forcibly involving the general public in the blockade program.

The Bangladesh Army continues its efforts in coordination with the civil administration and other law enforcement agencies to maintain peace, harmony, and stability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and to ensure the safety of the lives and property of local residents and tourists. ISPR informed that the Bangladesh Army will continue its efforts to maintain the peaceful environment of the hill region in the future.

Notably, yesterday, Wednesday, the Sajek Jan Adhikar Raksha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association announced a blockade for the third time on the Sajek tourism road. According to a statement from the organisations, the blockade would continue indefinitely starting today. Therefore, tourists were requested to leave Sajek by yesterday, Wedenday.

Following the blockade call by these regional organisations, the district administration announced the closure of Sajek for safety reasons.

In a public notice last evening, Rangamati Deputy Commissioner Nazma Ashrafi stated that the Sajek Valley tourist center in Baghaichhari Upazila would remain temporarily closed until further notice.

item.title: Dhaka-Chittagong rail services resume after 24 hours
item.description:
Train services on the Dhaka-bound line of the Dhaka-Chittagong route resumed at 12:50pm on Thursday, more than 24 hours after the Karnaphuli Commuter Express derailed in Comilla's Laksam.
The Bijoy Express, travelling from Chittagong to Mymensingh, was the first train to cross the accident site after the line reopened.
Omar Faruk Bhuiyan, station master of Laksam Railway Junction, said train services were now operating normally on both lines.
The damaged track was repaired by 7am on Thursday, but services remained suspended on the Dhaka-bound line because a derailed coach was found. During the suspension, trains in both directions used the other line, causing some disruption. The Chattala Express, bound for Dhaka, and the Paharika Express, bound for Sylhet, passed through Laksam at 10:23am and 10:48am, respectively, on Thursday.
The accident occurred around 12:30pm on Wednesday in the outer section of Naoti station, near Azgara Bazar in Laksam, when five coaches of the Karnaphuli Commuter Express and three wheels of its engine derailed. At least seven passengers were injured.
A rescue train from Chittagong reached the site on Wednesday evening. Recovery work was completed around 5am on Thursday, followed by track repairs.
Meanwhile, railway authorities suspended sub-assistant engineer Sarwar Alam over allegations that he failed to inform the control room about repair work underway at the accident site. He was responsible for the Feni region under the Eastern Railway’s engineering department.
A four-member committee has been formed to investigate the accident, Chittagong Divisional Railway Manager Mostafizur Rahman Bhuiyan said on Wednesday night.

The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified both of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,103, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the two new suspected fatalities, both were recorded in Dhaka.
A total of 995 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Thursday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 217,760.
During the same period, 36 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 23,248.

item.title: 4,157 killed in nine months as nation marks Road Safety Day
item.description:
Twelve people died in a head-on collision in Natore on Tuesday. According to police and surviving passengers, the bus was being driven by its supervisor while the regular driver slept in the back.
Two days later, Bangladesh is observing National Road Safety Day with the familiar program of seminars, discussions and promises to make its roads safer.
The latest figures offer little reason for reassurance.
At least 4,157 people were killed and 5,391 injured in 4,285 road crashes between January and September this year, according to the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA). That is an average of more than 15 deaths every day.
This year’s observance, under the theme “Safe Roads, Prosperous Nation, Bangladesh First,” comes amid persistent concerns over unfit vehicles, unqualified drivers and the failure to enforce existing traffic laws.
The Natore crash brought several of those concerns into sharp focus.
Police and injured passengers said the RP Special Paribahan bus was heading towards Bonpara when its supervisor, Sohel Rana, took over the wheel after a stop at Ishwardi around 3am.
Ramjan Ali, a surviving passenger from Chapainawabganj, said the regular driver left his seat after the break. About an hour later, the bus collided with a truck, killing 12 people and injuring at least 25.
The circumstances of the crash have once again raised questions about who is allowed to drive passenger buses and how effectively transport operators are monitored.
The deaths in Natore are part of a much larger toll.
According to Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity, at least 125,405 people were killed in 72,736 road crashes between 2013 and 2025. Another 176,249 people were left permanently disabled, the organisation said.
Children have been among the worst affected. Road Safety Foundation figures show that 7,963 children died in road crashes between January 2020 and September 2026.
Nearly 3,000 of them were killed in motorcycle crashes, while 2,812 died as pedestrians.
Yet the problems identified by successive governments and road safety experts remain largely unresolved.
BRTA records indicate that around 650,000 vehicles are operating without the required registration, route permits or fitness certificates. More than 75,000 buses and trucks have exceeded their prescribed economic lifespan.
The shortage of qualified professional drivers for heavy and medium vehicles is estimated at around 30%.
Vehicle fitness is another major concern. Around 70% of buses and minibuses in Dhaka and other major cities reportedly lack valid fitness documents.
Driver health also receives inadequate attention. At a BRTA and Dhaka Ahsania Mission health camp in 2023, around 73% of 541 drivers who underwent eye examinations were found to need glasses.
In 2019, the National Road Safety Council identified seven priority areas and made 111 recommendations to improve road safety.
Experts say there has been little visible progress in implementing them.
BUET Assistant Professor Kazi Md Saifun Newaz said the country already has the Road Transport Act 2018 and Road Transport Rules 2022, but legislation alone cannot prevent crashes.
“Everyone knows the causes of road crashes and their remedies. What is missing is consistent and coordinated action,” he said.
“Observing days will not solve anything.”
The BRTA says it has filed more than 110,000 cases through mobile courts and joint enforcement drives in the first nine months of this year, targeting unfit vehicles, invalid licences, speeding and other violations.
But the continuing death toll raises questions about whether these drives are producing lasting improvements.
Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity Secretary General Mozammel Haque Chowdhury blamed institutional inefficiency, corruption and the influence of transport owners’ and workers’ groups for the persistent disorder.
Road Safety Foundation Executive Director Saidur Rahman said the dangers were particularly acute for children on rural roads, where vehicles frequently pass close to homes and enforcement is weak.
“The authorities know the causes and the consequences, but there is no remedy,” he said.
The government has pledged to enact a comprehensive road safety law by December 2027.
The proposed Road Safety Act 2026 includes free emergency treatment for crash victims, legal protection for people who assist the injured, a demerit-point system for traffic offenders and higher penalties for repeat violations.
Road Transport and Bridges Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam has also reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to the UN target of halving road deaths and serious injuries by 2030.
For now, the country enters another Road Safety Day with thousands of lives lost, longstanding recommendations awaiting implementation and another deadly crash exposing the dangers on its highways.

item.title: Ukraine and Russia trade strikes following Witkoff talks
item.description:
Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight, authorities from both countries said on Thursday, shortly after US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg.
Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, wounding tens of residents, city authorities said.
In an update later in the morning, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had fired 21 missiles towards 12 regions in Ukraine. In Kyiv region, the strikes killed two people and injured 34 others, including five children.
The subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro river in Kyiv was also damaged, Mayor ⁠Vitali ​Klitschko ​said ​on Telegram.
“Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential Areas,” Ukrainian foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.
His post referred to Witkoff recently calling Putin a “humanitarian” for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday. Hubbard had been captured by Russian forces and jailed over charges of being a mercenary.
The Ukrainian foreign minister added: “Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”
Another Russian strike killed a woman and injured four others in the Kharkiv region in northeast Ukraine, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram. A drone also hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in the Poltava region, local authorities said without providing more details.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, with many targeting Moscow.
At least two people were killed in the Ukrainian strikes on Russia.
In western Russia’s Lipetsk city, a man was injured as drones hit apartment buildings and a medical facility, Governor Igor Artamonov said on Telegram.
The latest round of strikes came after US special envoy Witkoff held talks with Zelensky in Norway earlier this week, followed by talks with Putin in Russia on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has attempted to mediate between the two sides to end the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Putin agreed “in principle” to resume US-mediated peace talks with Kyiv as soon as next month. Zelensky, too, said on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for trilateral talks at the negotiators level to be held as soon as possible.
It was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war, US President Donald Trump claimed after Witkoff’s meeting with Putin. However, that did not stop the neighboring nations from keeping up a barrage of attacks.
“Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening,” Zelensky said in a post on social media on Thursday.
“It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war. But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps – steps toward ending the killing,” he said, once again advocating for stronger air defense capabilities and a faster supply of missiles from allies.

item.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi threat
item.description:
At least two people were killed in a strike on a Saudi airport in the eastern city of Dammam on Wednesday, as Washington ordered some diplomats and family members to leave the Gulf country.
Saudi Arabia’s revived war with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels has intensified in recent weeks, with the Yemeni rebels targeting several major Saudi airports.
The Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening killed two people and injured eight others.
The authority added on X that the extent of the material damage to the airport was being assessed.
It did not say who was behind the attack and the Houthis did not claim responsibility.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 said flights from the airport were being diverted as operations came to a halt.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said forces successfully intercepted a drone targeting an oil facility, but that falling debris killed two people and injured two others. Those killed were identified by the ministry as a Filipino and a Nepali national.
Meanwhile, US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said his department had issued an order for the departure of non-essential staff and family members at the US embassy in Riyadh.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” Pigott wrote on X.
Both Reuters and AFP news agency cited unnamed sources as saying a similar order was also issued for other countries in the Gulf, with the AFP listing the UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain.
Pigott denied the reports, saying they were “inaccurate” and that only employees in Saudi Arabia were ordered to leave.
The US has issued similar evacuation orders on more than one occasion this year amid the Iran war and Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Tehran.
A four-year truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels collapsed amid the Iran war, with Saudi Arabia experiencing near daily attacks this month.

item.title: Son of Myanmar’s Suu Kyi says had first call in five years
item.description:
The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.
Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
AFP could not immediately reach Aris -- who lives in the United Kingdom -- and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.
However, he posted images accompanying his Facebook post which appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.
“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military held Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.
But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.
On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.
Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing -- who ousted Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup -- was earlier this year installed as civilian president.
Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

item.title: Bangladesh Bank website shut down to prevent cyberattacks
item.description:
The official website of Bangladesh Bank has been kept offline due to concerns over a possible cyber-attack.

However, internet banking and mobile banking transactions are functioning normally, so customers are not facing any issues with their transactions.

Regarding this, Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Arif Hossain Khan told Prothom Alo on Thursday night that the website is being checked for any faults.

This decision was made due to concerns about worldwide attacks. There are no problems for customers in their transactions as a result.

Currently, the internet and software are extremely important for delivering government services, banking, e-commerce, media, and various online platforms.

A significant portion of these websites relies on the PHP programming language. Recently, after two critical security flaws were identified in PHP, there has been global concern about cyber security.

According to BBC and Reuters reports, after two critical security flaws were found in PHP, a widely used programming language for developing and managing websites, various governments have taken emergency actions.

Following the news of the flaws, governments and commercial enterprises worldwide have shut down their websites since Wednesday night. Despite this, there have been millions of hacking attempts reported.

Using artificial intelligence (AI), a researcher has discovered two highly dangerous flaws in a programming language called PHP.

This programming language has been used in nearly 70 per cent of websites around the world.

BBC's cyber affairs correspondent, Joe Tidy, said that this is an unprecedented situation where IT teams have been scrambling to protect their organisations from a highly serious cyber attack risk, resulting in one website after another going offline.

For example, the Edinburgh Council website, the ''Doctor Who'' section of the BBC website, and websites of various companies in Japan, Belgium, and the Netherlands have been taken offline.

Even some cyber security authorities have taken their own websites offline although they were the ones trying to alert the public about its importance.

As a precaution to avoid potential risks of global cyber attacks, Bangladesh Bank has kept its website offline.
